name: Daria Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage a customer support team of 14 at Vellora, one of the big mobile and broadband companies. Most of my day is watching the queue: how many chats are waiting, how long people are on hold, who's stuck with an angry customer. Since spring I've also been running the pilot for our AI chat assistant, so half my week is reading through its conversations and flagging where it got things wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the pilot, honestly, it's the most interesting thing I've done since I started. What grinds me down is the rota, because people swap shifts and I'm doing the jigsaw at ten at night on my phone. I'm 27, I live on my own, and my grandmother left me a small studio flat that I rent out, so I'm in a comfortable spot money-wise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically our pilot if it stalls. The chat assistant handles password resets and bill dates fine, but anything with an upset customer still comes to a person. If it never gets better than that, my team stays about the size it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that took the dull tickets off us, which is true. Online I'd probably post a short thread about what the pilot actually taught us, because people overhype it in both directions. Friends would get the honest version: the chat assistant at my telecom job is a decent intern, not a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, if I'm honest. I've bet some of my career on being the person who knows how to run AI and people together. If it stays a tool, that's still useful, just less of a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the team and push the assistant into the next easy area, like order tracking. I'd put the rent from the studio into my savings and maybe start looking at a second small flat in a couple of years. And I'd keep an eye out for team lead roles at the bigger tech firms in town, because there are plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, like an exciting project that fizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a decent intern mean for your team day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means fewer of the dull tickets, so my people get more of the hard ones. That's actually tougher on them, because every chat is someone angry about a bill. Tomasz on my team said last month he misses the easy resets, because they were a breather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the studio income change how you think about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. The rent covers about a third of my own rent, so I never feel trapped at Vellora. I can push for things at work because I know I'd be fine for a long time if it went wrong.

say: AI is a **useful tool** that took the dull tickets off us.
I'd post a **short thread** on what the pilot really taught us.
The chat assistant is a **decent intern**, not a replacement.
think: I'd be **a little disappointed**, because I bet my career on AI plus people.
If AI stays a tool, my skill is still useful, just **less of a story**.
do: Push the assistant into **order tracking** next.
Put the **studio rent** into savings towards a second small flat.
Watch for **team lead roles** at the bigger tech firms in town.
feel: **Calm**, though a bit flat, like a project that fizzled.
S0.quote: The chat assistant at my telecom job is a decent intern, not a replacement.
fieldNote: She is **pulled towards change**, so a plateau disappoints her more than it relieves her.

Save the studio rent towards a second small flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the version I actually expect. Answering customers is right there on the card, and that's my whole team. I'd guess half the chats go to the assistant within two years, and the team gets smaller but busier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance to design the new team properly instead of having it done to us. I'd probably speak at the internal town hall about it, because I've got the pilot data. Online I'd write about how you keep humans on the hard calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, steady AI change is good for me and bad for about six of the 14 people on my support team. Somebody has to run the mix of AI and humans, check the quality and handle the escalations, and that's me. But I'm not naive, the headcount goes from 14 to eight and I'm the one who signs that off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the plan for the new team myself in the first three months, before someone in finance writes a worse one. I'd get two of my people trained as AI quality reviewers so they have a new job rather than no job. And I'd take an online course on conversation design, which is basically writing how the bot talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. It's a strange mix to sit with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the six you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who are great on the phone but hate screens, mainly. Marta has been there nine years and she can calm anyone down, but she types with two fingers. I'd fight for her as an escalation handler, because the angriest calls will always need someone like her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign it off. What would you say to them on the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, as early as I'm allowed. I'd rather tell them in January that changes are coming than have them find out from a rumour in March. And I'd sit with each one and look at what they could move into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's different. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then it can also do my bit: check the quality, write the rota, decide who handles what. Managing a support team is all thinking work, so the robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that companies need to slow the rollout and keep people on while the rules catch up. At work I'd still be the AI person, because walking away from that would be silly. Online I'd probably be more careful than usual, because everyone would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job lasts maybe a year past 2028, as the person who switches the old system off. After that, a big company doesn't need a support manager when there's no support team. I'm not in danger financially for a long time, but the career I was building would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my car and start looking at a second rental flat straight away, before prices move. I'd use my savings and the studio as a base and try to get into a role at one of the AI firms themselves, doing customer operations for their business clients. I'd also stop the conversation design course, because that skill would be automated before I finished it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky, but not lost. I've got a cushion, it's my plans that would wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy property when everything's shifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people still need somewhere to live, and a flat is a real thing. I watched what my grandmother's studio did for me. I'd rather own two small flats than have my savings sitting in a bank while everything else moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your team in that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't know any more than they do, honestly. I'd tell them to save what they can and not to sign up for any big loans. It would be the first time I've ever told them I didn't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to get ahead of it, which is how I like it. I'd be 32, and I'd want to be on the side that builds these systems, not the side they replace. The worry is that by 2031 even that side gets thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a five-year transition and we should treat it like one: plan it, fund it, be honest about it. At Vellora I'd pitch a proper retraining plan for the whole support floor. With friends I'd say start moving now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do well for about four years, running the switch-over and probably getting promoted for it. Then in 2031 the AI can run the switch-over itself. So five years of warning buys me time and money, but not a safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask to lead the full rollout across all three support sites, which would mean a promotion and more pay. I'd save most of the pay rise and buy a second small flat by year two. And I'd look hard at work with a hands-on part, maybe running a team of broadband installation engineers, since robots there come about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit uneasy, like I'm running fast on a moving walkway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An installation team? That's a long way from chat queues.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but the engineers who go into people's homes are the hardest thing Vellora has to automate. Someone has to schedule them, deal with the angry customer at the door and keep the vans moving. I'd do a six-month secondment there first to see if I'm any good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you skip spending on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd skip the new car I'd been eyeing and holidays would be shorter. I'd rather have the second flat paid down than a nice car parked outside a job I might lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I can work with that. I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd have had time to build something that doesn't depend on one employer. That's the one I'd almost welcome, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if we start now, and that it's on companies to retrain people, not just cut them. I'd encourage my team to treat the next five years as paid learning time. Online I'd probably write a lot about it, because people would want practical advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out fine. By 2036 I'd want three small flats and a stake in something, maybe a small firm that sets up AI support for local businesses. My income wouldn't depend on Vellora needing a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy the second flat and start a side business on weekends, setting up chat assistants for small shops and clinics in town. I'd stay at Vellora for the steady pay and to learn from the big rollout. Around 2030 I'd decide whether the side business is big enough to go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small knot. The knot is my team, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the knot.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my team don't have a studio flat from their grandmother. Ten years sounds like a lot until you're 45 with a mortgage and your whole skill set is answering broadband questions. I'd feel responsible for making sure they used the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a business setting up AI also at risk once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, by 2036 probably. That's why the flats matter more in the long run. My side business setting up chatbots is the bridge, and my rental flats are the floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be broke, I wouldn't, but because everything I've built my career on would be useless before I'd had a chance to use it. What would help is companies giving people real notice, at least a year, and paying for retraining that leads to an actual job. And for my team, some help with income while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how weird it is to be the person bringing the AI in. People at work think I'm either a traitor or a genius for bringing the AI in, and I'm neither. I'm just someone who'd rather steer the thing than stand in front of it.
